items.question: In question 16, $A = 25^\circ$, $a = 11$ cm, and $c = 27$ cm. Explain why no triangle $\triangle ABC$ can be formed, using the sine rule and the range of possible values for $\sin C$.
items.referenceAnswer: Using the sine rule: $\frac{c}{\sin C} = \frac{a}{\sin A}$, so $\sin C = \frac{c \sin A}{a} = \frac{27 \sin 25^\circ}{11} \approx 1.04$. Since $\sin C > 1$, which is impossible, no such triangle exists.
missedPoints: Uses sine rule correctly to set up equation
States that sin C > 1 is impossible
Concludes no triangle can be formed

items.question: In question 17, $A = 74^\circ$, $a = 16$ cm, $c = 9$ cm. Show that exactly one triangle can be formed, and find $C$ correct to one decimal place.
items.referenceAnswer: Using $\frac{c}{\sin C} = \frac{a}{\sin A}$, we get $\sin C = \frac{9 \sin 74^\circ}{16} \approx 0.540$, so $C \approx 32.7^\circ$. Since $A = 74^\circ$ is acute and $a > c$, only one triangle is possible — the obtuse solution $C \approx 147^\circ$ is rejected because $A + C > 180^\circ$.

items.subject: math
items.question: In question 18, $B = 135^\circ$, $c = 7$ cm, $b = 2$ cm. Explain why no triangle can be formed, referencing the sine rule and the maximum possible value of sine.
items.referenceAnswer: Applying the sine rule: $\frac{c}{\sin C} = \frac{b}{\sin B}$, so $\sin C = \frac{c \sin B}{b} = \frac{7 \sin 135^\circ}{2} \approx 2.47$. Since $\sin C > 1$, which is outside the valid range $[0,1]$, no triangle exists.

items.question: In the first worked example (line 15), $\theta$ is obtuse and $\frac{13}{\sin A} = \frac{8}{\sin 17^\circ}$. Given $A = 28.4^\circ$, explain how $\theta = 135^\circ$ is obtained, and verify that $\theta$ is indeed obtuse.
items.referenceAnswer: Since angles in a triangle sum to $180^\circ$, $\theta = 180^\circ - A - 17^\circ = 180^\circ - 28.4^\circ - 17^\circ = 134.6^\circ \approx 135^\circ$. As $135^\circ > 90^\circ$, $\theta$ is obtuse, satisfying the given condition.

items.question: Compare the outcomes of questions 16 and 18: both give $\sin(\text{angle}) > 1$. What do their given angle–side pairs have in common that leads to this impossibility?
items.referenceAnswer: In both cases, the side opposite the given angle is too short to reach the other side: in Q16, side $a = 11$ cm is too short to form a triangle with angle $A = 25^\circ$ and side $c = 27$ cm; in Q18, side $b = 2$ cm is too short opposite the large obtuse angle $B = 135^\circ$ and side $c = 7$ cm. In both, the sine rule yields $\sin(\text{angle}) > 1$, violating the fundamental bound of sine.
